def: To happen or make something happen faster

def: To agree with or match something else

def: To gradually increase in amount or collect over time

def: To change something, or to become different

def: To examine something in detail to understand or explain it

def: To begin to exist or happen as a result of something

def: To judge the size, quality or importance of something

def: To connect someone or something with something else in your mind

def: To accept something as true without having proof

def: To show or prove that something is true

def: To consider one thing in relation to another

def: To be useful to someone, or to gain an advantage from something

def: To support or strengthen something

def: To increase or improve something

def: To find a number or amount using mathematics

def: To adjust a measuring instrument so that it gives accurate results

def: To make people doubt something or see it differently

def: To cause or speed up an important change or process

ex.base: Enzymes catalyse thousands of chemical reactions inside living cells.
ex.past: The crisis catalysed major reforms in banking regulation.
ex.part: Social change has often been catalysed by technological innovation.

def: To put people or things into groups according to their features

ex.base: Researchers categorise responses according to their main theme.
ex.past: The study categorised participants into three age groups.

def: To make something happen, especially something bad

def: To question whether something is true, right or acceptable

def: To describe or be the typical feature of something

ex.part: The period was characterised by rapid industrial growth.

def: To mention something as an example, reason or source

ex.base: Many respondents cite cost as the main barrier to healthy eating.

def: To say that something is true, although it has not been proved

def: To make something clearer or easier to understand

def: To arrange things into groups according to shared qualities

def: To rise gradually to a higher level or amount

def: To exist together at the same time or in the same place

def: To happen at the same time, or to be the same as something

def: To fall suddenly and dramatically in value or number

def: To gather information from different sources and organise it

ex.part: The figures were collated from official government reports.

def: To gather data or samples in order to study them

def: To begin something, formally

def: To express an opinion or give an explanation about something

ex.part: The decline in reading has been widely commented on.

def: To examine the similarities and differences between two or more things

ex.base: This study compares urban and rural attitudes towards recycling.

def: To produce a list, report or set of data by collecting information

def: To add to something in a way that improves it or makes it complete

def: To make a difficult situation or problem even worse

ex.part: The crisis has been compounded by a shortage of skilled staff.

def: To consist of particular parts, or to form a proportion of a whole

def: To weaken or harm something such as safety, quality or health

def: To calculate an answer or amount, often using a computer

def: To admit, often unwillingly, that something is true

ex.base: Even critics concede that the policy has reduced unemployment.

ex.part: It must be conceded that the sample size was small.

def: To form an idea or theoretical model of something

ex.base: Many scholars conceptualise poverty as a lack of opportunity.

ex.part: Wellbeing has been conceptualised in many different ways.

def: To decide something is true after considering the evidence, or to end

def: To agree with someone or have the same opinion

ex.base: Most experts concur that urgent action on climate change is needed.

def: To organise and carry out a study, survey or experiment

def: To match or obey a rule, standard or pattern

def: To think about or discuss something carefully

def: To be made of or formed from particular parts

def: To form or be a particular part or proportion of something

def: To ask for advice or look at a source for information

def: To disagree with something formally or say that it is wrong

def: To become smaller in size or amount

def: To communicate information, ideas or feelings

def: To match or be similar or equal to something

def: To provide evidence that supports a statement or theory

def: To say what you think is wrong or bad about something

def: To consider or judge something in a particular way

def: To reduce something to the smallest possible amount

ex.base: Careful planning minimises the environmental impact of new buildings.
ex.past: The company minimised waste by recycling all its packaging.
ex.part: The risk of infection has been minimised through strict hygiene rules.

def: To be very similar to something or show it clearly

ex.base: Trends in Canada closely mirror those in the United States.
ex.past: The fall in sales mirrored the wider economic slowdown.
ex.part: This pattern is mirrored in most developed economies.

def: To make something harmful less severe

ex.base: Governments must mitigate the effects of rising sea levels.
ex.past: The new policy mitigated some of the damage caused by the floods.
ex.part: The risks have been mitigated by stricter controls.

def: To create a mathematical or computer representation of a system

ex.base: Economists model how interest rates affect household spending.
ex.past: The team modelled the spread of the virus across Europe.
ex.part: Future sea levels have been modelled under different emission scenarios.

def: To watch and check something regularly over a period of time

ex.base: Satellites monitor changes in Arctic sea ice throughout the year.
ex.past: Doctors monitored the patients for six months after the treatment.
ex.part: Water quality in the river is monitored on a weekly basis.

def: To increase greatly in number or amount

ex.base: Bacteria multiply rapidly in warm and humid conditions.
ex.past: The number of mobile phone users multiplied in the early 2000s.
ex.part: The risks of flooding have multiplied as cities have expanded.

def: To become smaller in difference or range

ex.base: The gender pay gap narrows as women reach senior positions.
ex.past: The gap between urban and rural incomes narrowed after 2005.
ex.part: The achievement gap has narrowed but has not disappeared.

def: To make something necessary

ex.base: An ageing population necessitates greater investment in healthcare.
ex.past: The rise in student numbers necessitated the construction of new campuses.
ex.part: Major reforms have been necessitated by the economic crisis.

def: To mention something because it is important or interesting

ex.base: The author notes that urban gardens improve community wellbeing.
ex.past: Smith (2019) noted a sharp rise in youth unemployment.
ex.part: It should be noted that the data were self-reported.

def: To say that you disagree with or oppose something

ex.base: Many residents object to the construction of new wind farms.
ex.past: Local farmers objected to the proposed motorway through their land.
ex.part: Environmental groups have objected to the expansion of the airport.

def: To notice or state something based on what has been seen or studied

ex.base: Teachers observe that students concentrate better after physical activity.
ex.past: The researchers observed a significant increase in bird populations.
ex.part: Similar patterns have been observed in other European cities.

def: To get something, especially through effort or a process

ex.base: Researchers must obtain informed consent from all participants before the study.
ex.past: The team obtained similar results using a much larger sample.
ex.part: The data were obtained from national census records.

def: To balance one effect with an opposite one

ex.base: Higher productivity can offset the cost of rising wages.
ex.past: Last year, gains in exports offset the decline in domestic demand.
ex.part: The losses were partly offset by increased tourism revenue.

def: To disagree with a plan or policy and try to stop it

ex.base: Many teachers oppose the use of standardised tests in primary schools.
ex.past: Several developing countries opposed the new trade agreement at the summit.
ex.part: The plan has been opposed by environmental campaigners.

def: To arrange ideas or information in a clear, logical order

ex.base: Good writers organise their ideas into clear, focused paragraphs.
ex.past: The author organised the chapters in chronological order.
ex.part: The report is organised into four main sections.

def: To describe the main facts or points without giving details

ex.base: This section outlines the methods used to collect the data.
ex.past: The minister outlined plans to reform the tax system.
ex.part: The main arguments are outlined in the introduction.

def: To be greater in number than another group

ex.base: Female students now outnumber male students at most universities.
ex.past: Imports outnumbered exports for the first time in 1985.
ex.part: Urban residents have outnumbered rural ones since 2007.

def: To achieve better results than someone or something else

ex.base: Girls consistently outperform boys in national reading tests.
ex.past: Private schools outperformed state schools in the 2019 exams.
ex.part: Solar energy has outperformed expectations in recent years.

def: To become larger, faster or more successful than something else

ex.base: Demand for housing far outstrips supply in many large cities.
ex.past: Population growth outstripped food production in the 1960s.
ex.part: Wage growth has been outstripped by rising living costs.

def: To be greater or more important than something else

ex.base: In my view, the benefits of tourism outweigh its drawbacks.
ex.past: The advantages of the scheme outweighed its initial costs.
ex.part: Any risks are outweighed by the potential health benefits.

def: To think something is larger or more important than it really is

ex.base: Many people overestimate how much exercise they actually do each week.
ex.past: Early forecasts overestimated the demand for electric vehicles.
ex.part: The benefits of the scheme may have been overestimated.

def: To share some features, areas or ideas with something else

ex.base: The two academic disciplines overlap in several important areas.
ex.past: The research interests of the two teams overlapped considerably.
ex.part: Their responsibilities have overlapped since the two departments merged.

def: To become greater or more successful than something else

ex.base: Online sales may soon overtake in-store sales in many countries.
ex.past: China overtook Japan as the world's second-largest economy in 2010.
ex.part: Coal has been overtaken by gas as the main source of electricity.

def: To put two people or things together, often to compare them

ex.base: The study pairs each participant with a partner of similar age.
ex.past: Researchers paired each new student with an experienced mentor.
ex.part: Each treatment group was paired with a matching control group.

def: To be similar to something or happen at the same time

ex.base: The rise in obesity closely parallels the growth of fast food.
ex.past: In the twentieth century, economic growth paralleled improvements in public health.
ex.part: The increase in car ownership was paralleled by a decline in cycling.

def: To express what someone said or wrote using different words

ex.base: Good students paraphrase sources rather than copying them word for word.
ex.past: The writer paraphrased the original text without changing its meaning.
ex.part: All borrowed ideas have been paraphrased and properly referenced.

def: To reach the highest point or level

ex.base: Electricity demand typically peaks in the early evening on weekdays.
ex.past: Oil production peaked at 10 million barrels a day in 2018.
ex.part: Global emissions have not yet peaked, according to the report.

def: To notice or understand something in a particular way

ex.base: Many students perceive online learning as less engaging than lectures.
ex.past: Most respondents perceived the new tax as unfair to poorer families.
ex.part: Nuclear power is often perceived as dangerous by the public.

def: To make a situation, belief or problem continue

ex.base: Some school textbooks still perpetuate outdated gender stereotypes about careers.
ex.past: The policy perpetuated inequalities between rural and urban schools.
ex.part: These myths have been perpetuated by popular media.

def: To make someone believe or do something by giving reasons
pattern: persuade sb to + verb / persuade sb that + clause

ex.base: Effective essays persuade the reader through clear and relevant evidence.
ex.past: The campaign persuaded thousands of people to stop smoking.
ex.part: Few voters have been persuaded by the government's arguments.

def: To test a new scheme or method on a small scale first

ex.base: Many universities pilot new teaching methods before introducing them more widely.
ex.past: The government piloted the programme in three northern cities.
ex.part: The questionnaire was piloted with a small group of volunteers.

def: To identify something exactly

ex.base: Genetic testing can pinpoint the source of the infection very quickly.
ex.past: The analysis pinpointed three regions with severe water shortages.
ex.part: The exact cause of the decline has not yet been pinpointed.

def: To stay at the same level after a period of growth

ex.base: Learning progress often plateaus after the first year of study.
ex.past: Life expectancy plateaued at around 81 years after 2015.
ex.part: Smartphone sales have plateaued in most developed markets.

def: To mark data on a graph or chart

ex.base: The graph plots average income against years of education.
ex.past: The researchers plotted temperature changes over a fifty-year period.
ex.part: The results are plotted on the vertical axis of the graph.

def: To fall suddenly and by a large amount

ex.base: Share prices often plummet when a company issues a profit warning.
ex.past: Fish stocks plummeted after decades of overfishing in the North Sea.
ex.part: Public trust in politicians has plummeted in recent years.

def: To fall suddenly and steeply

ex.base: Temperatures plunge well below zero during the polar winter.
ex.past: Exports plunged by 30 per cent during the financial crisis.
ex.part: Profits have plunged since the start of the trade dispute.

def: To suggest something as a basic fact for an argument or theory

ex.base: The theory posits that humans are naturally cooperative.
ex.past: Freud posited the existence of the unconscious mind.
ex.part: A link between stress and illness has been posited by many scholars.

def: To suggest a theory or idea as a basis for reasoning

ex.base: Some scientists postulate that life may exist on other planets.
ex.past: Einstein postulated that the speed of light is constant.
ex.part: It has been postulated that diet influences brain development.

def: To come before something in time or order

ex.base: A brief introduction precedes each chapter of the report.
ex.past: A long period of drought preceded the famine.
ex.part: The financial crisis was preceded by a housing boom.

def: To make something bad happen suddenly or sooner than expected

ex.base: Sudden rises in interest rates can precipitate a housing crash.
ex.past: The collapse of the bank precipitated a global financial crisis.
ex.part: The decline was precipitated by a sharp fall in commodity prices.

def: To say what will happen in the future based on evidence

ex.base: Experts predict that global demand for water will rise sharply.
ex.past: The model correctly predicted the outcome of the general election.
ex.part: The world population is predicted to reach ten billion by 2060.

def: To introduce a text or statement with something said first

ex.base: Writers often preface controversial claims with a note of caution.
ex.past: The author prefaced the study with a short historical overview.
ex.part: Each chapter is prefaced by a summary of its main points.

def: To believe something is true without full proof

ex.base: The model presumes that consumers always act rationally.
ex.past: Early researchers presumed that the disease was hereditary.
ex.part: It is often presumed that technology improves productivity.

def: To decide which things are most important and deal with them first

ex.base: In my opinion, governments should prioritise education over military spending.
ex.past: The council prioritised public transport in its annual budget.
ex.part: Patient safety must be prioritised above all other concerns.

def: To examine or ask questions in order to discover hidden facts

ex.base: The interviews probe participants' attitudes towards renewable energy and recycling.
ex.past: The study probed the reasons behind falling birth rates in Europe.
ex.part: These questions have been probed in several recent studies.

def: To calculate a future amount or trend from present data
pattern: project + noun / be projected to + verb

ex.base: Analysts project steady growth in renewable energy over the next decade.
ex.past: The report projected a sharp rise in housing costs.
ex.part: Car ownership is projected to double by 2040 in developing countries.

def: To increase rapidly in number

ex.base: Fake news stories proliferate on social media during elections.
ex.past: Private language schools proliferated across the region in the 1990s.
ex.part: Online courses have proliferated since the start of the pandemic.

def: To cause someone to take action or something to happen
pattern: prompt + noun / prompt sb to + verb

ex.base: Rising obesity rates prompt calls for a tax on sugary drinks.
ex.past: The findings prompted the government to review its policy.
ex.part: The study was prompted by concerns about teenage mental health.

def: To suggest an idea, plan or theory for others to consider

ex.base: This essay proposes a new approach to reducing traffic congestion.
ex.past: The committee proposed raising the minimum wage by five per cent.
ex.part: Several explanations have been proposed for the decline in bee populations.

def: To show that something is true using evidence

ex.base: No single study can prove that one teaching method is best.
ex.past: The experiment proved that the vaccine was safe for children.
ex.part: The link between smoking and cancer has been proven beyond doubt.

def: To cause a strong reaction, especially a negative one

ex.base: Proposals to raise fuel taxes often provoke strong public opposition.
ex.past: The decision provoked widespread protests across the country.
ex.part: Considerable controversy has been provoked by the new law.

def: To add details to a statement to make it less general

ex.base: Careful writers qualify their claims to avoid overgeneralisation.
ex.past: The author qualified her argument in the final chapter.
ex.part: These conclusions should be qualified by the limitations of the study.

def: To express or measure something as a number or amount

ex.base: This study quantifies the economic cost of traffic congestion.
ex.past: The researchers quantified the health benefits of cycling to work.
ex.part: The environmental damage has never been fully quantified.

def: To express doubt about whether something is true or valid

ex.base: Some experts question the reliability of online surveys.
ex.past: Critics questioned whether the policy would actually reduce crime.
ex.part: The accuracy of these figures has been questioned by economists.

def: To repeat the exact words of a writer or speaker
pattern: quote + noun / be quoted as saying

ex.base: Students should quote sources accurately and include page numbers.
ex.past: The article quoted several leading climate scientists from different countries.
ex.part: The minister was quoted as saying that taxes would rise.

def: To put things in order according to quality or importance
pattern: rank sth by sth / rank + adverb

ex.base: The index ranks countries according to their quality of life.
ex.past: Respondents ranked job security as their top priority.
ex.part: Finland has been ranked first for education several times.

def: To rise again after a fall

ex.base: Tourist numbers usually rebound quickly after a natural disaster.
ex.past: The economy rebounded strongly in the second half of the year.
ex.part: Consumer spending has rebounded to pre-pandemic levels in most regions.

def: To prove that a claim or criticism is false

ex.base: In the second section, the author rebuts each objection in turn.
ex.past: The minister rebutted claims that the hospital would close.
ex.part: These criticisms have been rebutted in several recent publications.

def: To repeat the main points of what has been said

ex.base: The final paragraph recaps the main points of the argument.
ex.past: The speaker recapped the key findings before taking questions.
ex.part: The main themes are recapped at the end of each chapter.

def: To advise that something should be done

ex.base: The report recommends that schools reduce class sizes in the early years.
ex.past: Doctors recommended limiting screen time for young children.
ex.part: It is recommended that adults exercise for 150 minutes per week.

def: To find a way to make two different ideas or facts agree

ex.base: Policymakers must reconcile economic growth with environmental protection.
ex.past: In her book, the author reconciled two apparently conflicting theories.
ex.part: These contradictory findings have never been fully reconciled.

def: To return to a normal level after a fall or difficult period

ex.base: Markets recover slowly after a major financial shock.
ex.past: House prices recovered gradually after the 2008 crash.
ex.part: The tourism industry has not fully recovered from the crisis.

def: To find and persuade people to take part in a study

ex.base: Clinical trials often struggle to recruit enough elderly participants.
ex.past: The researchers recruited 300 volunteers from local universities.
ex.part: Participants were recruited through online advertisements and social media.

def: To make something smaller in size, amount or degree

ex.base: Regular exercise significantly reduces the risk of heart disease.
ex.past: The city reduced traffic congestion by introducing a daily charge.
ex.part: Plastic bag use has been reduced by almost 90 per cent.

def: To mention or direct attention to a source or topic

ex.base: The term 'gig economy' refers to short-term, flexible work.
ex.past: The author referred to several earlier studies in her introduction.
ex.part: This phenomenon is often referred to as 'brain drain'.

def: To prove that a statement, theory or claim is wrong

ex.base: New evidence refutes the claim that vaccines cause autism.
ex.past: The scientist refuted the theory with detailed experimental data.
ex.part: This assumption has been refuted by numerous studies.

def: To make an idea, argument or feeling stronger

ex.base: These findings reinforce the argument for early intervention.
ex.past: The survey results reinforced earlier concerns about student debt.
ex.part: Traditional gender roles are often reinforced through advertising.

def: To repeat something in order to emphasise it

ex.base: The conclusion reiterates the need for further research in this area.
ex.past: The minister reiterated her commitment to cutting emissions.
ex.part: This point has been reiterated by many health experts.

def: To refuse to accept or agree with an idea, claim or proposal

ex.base: Most scientists reject the idea that intelligence is fixed at birth.
ex.past: Voters rejected the proposal in a national referendum.
ex.part: The null hypothesis was rejected at the five per cent level.

def: To show or have a connection between two things
pattern: relate sth to sth / relate to sth

ex.base: This essay relates income levels to educational achievement.
ex.past: The researchers related crime rates to levels of unemployment.
ex.part: Chronic stress is closely related to poor physical health.

def: To say or write something as a comment
pattern: remark that + clause / remark on sth

ex.base: Several reviewers remark on the originality of the study.
ex.past: One participant remarked that the course was too theoretical.
ex.part: It has frequently been remarked that wealth does not guarantee happiness.

def: To cause something to be in a particular state or condition

ex.base: Rapid technological change renders many traditional skills obsolete.
ex.past: The drought rendered large areas of farmland unusable.
ex.part: Many antibiotics have been rendered ineffective by overuse.

def: To express something again using different words

ex.base: Strong candidates rephrase the question in their introduction.
ex.past: The researcher rephrased the question to avoid confusion.
ex.part: Several survey items were rephrased after the pilot study.

def: To repeat a study to see if the same results are obtained

ex.base: Scientists must replicate these findings before they can be widely accepted.
ex.past: A second team replicated the experiment and obtained similar results.
ex.part: The original findings have been replicated in several different countries.

def: To give information about findings or events

ex.base: Most respondents report higher stress levels at work than at home.
ex.past: The authors reported a 15 per cent improvement in test scores.
ex.part: Similar effects have been reported in older adults.

def: To look like or be similar to something

ex.base: The symptoms of the disease resemble those of the common cold.
ex.past: Early computers resembled large industrial machines rather than modern laptops.
ex.part: Political debate has increasingly resembled entertainment in recent years.

def: To say something again, often more clearly or strongly

ex.base: A strong conclusion restates the thesis in different words.
ex.past: The author restated her position in the final chapter.
ex.part: The main argument is restated briefly in the conclusion.

def: To cause a particular outcome, or happen because of something
pattern: result in + noun/-ing / result from sth

ex.base: Deforestation results in the loss of countless animal habitats.
ex.past: The new regulations resulted in a sharp drop in road accidents.
ex.part: Overfishing has resulted in the collapse of several fish stocks.

def: To find and bring back stored information

ex.base: The software can retrieve patient records in a matter of seconds.
ex.past: Researchers retrieved archival documents from the national library.
ex.part: All relevant studies were retrieved from three online databases.

def: To make known something that was previously hidden or unknown

ex.base: The figures reveal a widening gap between rich and poor households.
ex.past: The survey revealed that most teenagers sleep less than eight hours.
ex.part: Brain scans have revealed clear changes in memory function.

def: To increase in number, level or amount

ex.base: Sea levels rise as polar ice continues to melt.
ex.past: Life expectancy rose steadily throughout the last century.
ex.part: The cost of living has risen faster than wages.

def: To be as good, large or important as something else

ex.base: Few cities rival London as a centre for international finance.
ex.past: In the 1980s, Japan's economy rivalled that of the United States.
ex.part: Its influence has rarely been rivalled by other universities.

def: To increase very quickly and suddenly

ex.base: Energy prices rocket whenever supplies are seriously disrupted.
ex.past: Demand for face masks rocketed in early 2020.
ex.part: Rents have rocketed in major cities over the past decade.

def: To select a group from a population in order to study it

ex.base: Researchers usually sample a small proportion of the wider population.
ex.past: The study sampled 1,200 households across five different regions.
ex.part: Water was sampled from twenty sites along the river.

def: To examine something very carefully to find any problems

ex.base: Peer reviewers scrutinise the methodology of every submitted paper.
ex.past: The parliamentary committee scrutinised the company's environmental record in detail.
ex.part: Government spending has been closely scrutinised by the media.

def: To divide something into separate parts or groups for analysis

ex.base: Marketers segment consumers by age, income and lifestyle.
ex.past: The analysts segmented the data by region and gender.
ex.part: The population was segmented into five income groups.

def: To keep things apart or treat them as different

ex.base: Good researchers separate fact from opinion when reviewing sources.
ex.past: The study separated participants into two distinct age groups.
ex.part: Personal and professional data must be separated for privacy reasons.

def: To prove or make clear that something is true

ex.base: Studies show that early reading improves later academic success.
ex.past: The experiment showed that plants grow faster under blue light.
ex.part: Exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of depression.

def: To become smaller in size or amount

ex.base: Glaciers shrink each year as global temperatures rise.
ex.past: The manufacturing sector shrank by a third during the 1980s.
ex.part: The rural population has shrunk considerably since 1950.

def: To be a sign of something or have a particular meaning

ex.base: Rising house prices often signify a strengthening economy.
ex.past: The election result signified a major shift in public opinion.
ex.part: Such changes have long signified the start of an economic downturn.

def: To guide readers by showing how a text is organised

ex.base: Effective writers signpost each new stage of their argument.
ex.past: The author signposted the main sections with clear headings.
ex.part: The structure of the essay is clearly signposted in the introduction.

def: To copy the conditions of a real situation, often by computer

ex.base: Climate models simulate how temperatures may change over the next century.
ex.past: Engineers simulated an earthquake to test the building's design.
ex.part: Several flooding scenarios have been simulated using advanced software.

def: To fall suddenly in price, value or number

ex.base: Car sales slump whenever fuel prices rise significantly.
ex.past: Investment slumped to its lowest level in twenty years.
ex.part: Demand for coal has slumped across Western Europe.

def: To rise very quickly to a high level

ex.base: Food prices soar when harvests fail across several major producers.
ex.past: Enrolment in online courses soared during the pandemic.
ex.part: Global temperatures have soared to record highs this decade.

def: To state something clearly and in exact detail

ex.base: The guidelines specify the minimum number of words required.
ex.past: The contract specified a completion date of March 2024.
ex.part: The criteria were clearly specified before the study began.

def: To form opinions about something without enough evidence
pattern: speculate that + clause / speculate about sth

ex.base: Some researchers speculate that the downward trend will soon reverse.
ex.past: Journalists speculated about the causes of the market crash.
ex.part: It has been speculated that the virus originated in bats.

def: To encourage something to happen faster or more strongly
pattern: spur + noun / spur sb to + verb

ex.base: Government grants spur innovation in the clean energy sector.
ex.past: The oil crisis spurred research into alternative fuels.
ex.part: Economic growth has been spurred by foreign investment.

def: To become steady and stop changing

ex.base: Inflation usually stabilises once interest rates are raised.
ex.past: The exchange rate stabilised after the central bank intervened.
ex.part: Unemployment has stabilised at around six per cent.

def: To stop developing, growing or improving

ex.base: Economies often stagnate when investment in education declines.
ex.past: Real wages stagnated for most of the decade.
ex.part: Labour productivity has stagnated in many economies since the financial crisis.

def: To express something clearly and formally in speech or writing

ex.base: The law states that all children must attend school until sixteen.
ex.past: The report stated that emissions had fallen by 12 per cent.
ex.part: As stated in the introduction, the study focuses on urban areas.

def: To originate from or be caused by something

ex.base: Many health problems stem from poor living conditions.
ex.past: The conflict stemmed from a long-standing dispute over water.
ex.part: Much of the recent unrest has stemmed from rising food prices.

def: To encourage something to grow, develop or become more active

ex.base: Lower taxes may stimulate consumer spending in the short term.
ex.past: The investment stimulated growth in the manufacturing sector.
ex.part: Demand for housing has been stimulated by cheaper credit.

def: To make an argument, case or position more convincing

ex.base: Reliable statistics strengthen any argument in an academic essay.
ex.past: The new data strengthened the case for a sugar tax.
ex.part: The theory has been strengthened by recent archaeological discoveries.

def: To give special importance to a point or idea

ex.base: The authors stress the importance of early diagnosis and treatment.
ex.past: The minister stressed that the cuts were only temporary.
ex.part: The need for international cooperation has been repeatedly stressed.

def: To arrange the parts of an essay or argument in a clear order

ex.base: Most students structure their essays around three main arguments.
ex.past: The author structured the report around four key themes.
ex.part: The interview was structured to encourage open responses.

def: To provide evidence to show that a claim is true

ex.base: Researchers must substantiate their claims with reliable evidence.
ex.past: Later studies with larger samples substantiated the original findings.
ex.part: These allegations have not been substantiated by any evidence.

def: To indicate that something is likely to be true

ex.base: Recent evidence suggests that sugar may be as harmful as fat.
ex.past: The findings suggested a link between social media use and anxiety.
ex.part: It has been suggested that a four-day week increases productivity.

def: To express the most important facts or ideas briefly

ex.base: The final section summarises the key findings of the research.
ex.past: The author summarised the main arguments in the conclusion.
ex.part: The results of the survey are summarised in Table 1.

def: To replace something older or less effective

ex.base: New technologies supersede older ones at an ever faster rate.
ex.past: In the early 2000s, digital cameras quickly superseded traditional film cameras.
ex.part: This theory has since been superseded by more accurate models.

def: To provide evidence that helps to show something is true

ex.base: The evidence strongly supports the view that diet affects mood.
ex.past: The results of the experiment supported the original hypothesis.
ex.part: This argument is supported by data from several countries.

def: To increase suddenly and strongly

ex.base: Electricity use surges during summer heatwaves in southern Europe.
ex.past: Applications to nursing courses surged by 30 per cent.
ex.part: Interest in electric cars has surged over the past two years.

def: To be greater or better than something or someone

ex.base: Global energy demand may soon surpass current production capacity.
ex.past: Sales surpassed expectations in the final quarter of the year.
ex.part: The previous temperature record has been surpassed three times this decade.

def: To ask many people questions to find out their opinions or habits

ex.base: The national census surveys every household in the country once a decade.
ex.past: The researchers surveyed 2,000 adults about their reading habits.
ex.part: Over half of the students surveyed reported high levels of stress.

def: To make something continue over a period of time

ex.base: Healthy ecosystems sustain a wide variety of plant and animal life.
ex.past: Strong exports sustained the national economy during the recession.
ex.part: Growth cannot be sustained without investment in skills.

def: To combine separate ideas or findings into a single whole

ex.base: A good literature review synthesises findings from many different studies.
ex.past: The authors synthesised data from forty published clinical trials.
ex.part: Evidence from various disciplines has been synthesised in this report.

def: To arrange data in a table

ex.base: Researchers tabulate the responses before carrying out statistical tests.
ex.past: The team tabulated the results by age group and gender.
ex.part: The main findings are tabulated below for easy comparison.

def: To give a particular name or description to something
pattern: term sth + noun / be termed + noun

ex.base: Economists term this situation a 'liquidity trap' in their analyses.
ex.past: Early researchers termed the condition 'shell shock' during the First World War.
ex.part: This phenomenon has been termed 'digital addiction' by some psychologists.

def: To use a procedure to check whether something is true or works

ex.base: This experiment tests whether caffeine improves short-term memory in adults.
ex.past: The team tested the vaccine on more than 30,000 volunteers.
ex.part: The new drug has been tested extensively in clinical trials.

def: To develop ideas in order to explain something
pattern: theorise that + clause / theorise about sth

ex.base: Some psychologists theorise that personality is largely inherited.
ex.past: Early economists theorised about the causes of inflation.
ex.part: It has been theorised that the universe will continue expanding forever.

def: To reach a particular amount when added together

ex.base: The country's annual imports total around 400 billion dollars.
ex.past: Government spending on health totalled 150 billion pounds in 2020.
ex.part: By 2015, losses had totalled more than five million euros.

def: To find the origin or development of something

ex.base: Historians trace the roots of the welfare state to the 1940s.
ex.past: Scientists traced the outbreak to a contaminated water supply.
ex.part: The decline has been traced to changes in farming practices.

def: To follow the development or progress of something over time

ex.base: Longitudinal studies track the same individuals over many years.
ex.past: The study tracked graduates' earnings for a decade after university.
ex.part: Household spending has been tracked since the early 1990s.

def: To change something completely, usually for the better

ex.base: Artificial intelligence transforms the way many companies operate.
ex.past: The internet transformed the way people access and share information.
ex.part: Healthcare has been transformed by new digital technologies.

def: To cause something to start suddenly

ex.base: Stressful events can trigger anxiety in young people.
ex.past: The report triggered a national debate on education funding.
ex.part: The crisis was triggered by a collapse in housing prices.

def: To become three times as large in amount or number

ex.base: Sales of solar panels triple roughly every five years.
ex.past: The number of international students tripled between 2000 and 2020.
ex.part: Average energy bills have almost tripled since 2021.

def: To think something is smaller or less important than it really is

ex.base: Many governments underestimate the long-term costs of an ageing population.
ex.past: Planners underestimated the number of commuters using the new line.
ex.part: The risks of climate change have been seriously underestimated.

def: To be the hidden cause or basis of something

ex.base: Complex social factors underlie the rise in youth crime.
ex.past: Economic insecurity underlay much of the political unrest of the 1930s.
ex.part: Similar assumptions have underlain government policy for decades.

def: To emphasise or draw attention to something important

ex.base: These findings underline the need for better public transport.
ex.past: The crisis underlined the importance of food security.
ex.part: The value of early education has been underlined by recent research.

def: To gradually make something weaker or less effective

ex.base: Widespread corruption undermines public trust in government institutions.
ex.past: The scandal undermined confidence in the banking system.
ex.part: Efforts to reduce poverty have been undermined by rising inflation.

def: To emphasise that something is important or true

ex.base: The report underscores the urgency of tackling plastic pollution.
ex.past: The floods underscored the need for better flood defences.
ex.part: The importance of trust has been underscored in numerous studies.

def: To begin and carry out a task, especially a large one

ex.base: Few organisations undertake research on such a large scale.
ex.past: The ministry undertook a full review of the national curriculum.
ex.part: A comprehensive survey of rural health was undertaken in 2019.

def: To support a principle or decision and keep it in place

ex.base: Democratic societies uphold the principle of free speech.
ex.past: The court upheld the ban on smoking in public places.
ex.part: The original ruling was upheld on appeal last year.

def: To prove that something is accurate, reliable or acceptable

ex.base: Field tests validate the accuracy of the computer model.
ex.past: The researchers validated the questionnaire with a small pilot group.
ex.part: The method has been validated in several clinical settings.

def: To be different in different situations or groups

ex.base: Life expectancy varies considerably between rich and poor regions.
ex.past: Responses varied according to the age and gender of participants.
ex.part: The results have varied widely across different studies.

def: To check that something is true or accurate

ex.base: Journalists should verify information carefully before publishing it online.
ex.past: A second laboratory later verified the original measurements and calculations.
ex.part: These claims have not been independently verified by other researchers.

def: To tell people about a possible danger or problem
pattern: warn that + clause / warn of sth

ex.base: Scientists warn that coral reefs could disappear by 2050.
ex.past: Economists warned of a recession if interest rates rose further.
ex.part: Governments have been warned about the risks of rising sea levels.

def: To make an action necessary or appropriate

ex.base: These unexpected results warrant further investigation by independent teams.
ex.past: The scale of the problem warranted urgent government action.
ex.part: Such a drastic response is not warranted by the evidence.

def: To make an argument or position less convincing or strong

ex.base: The small sample size weakens the study's conclusions.
ex.past: Inconsistent data weakened the case for the new policy.
ex.part: The argument is weakened by a lack of reliable evidence.

def: To consider facts or arguments carefully before deciding
pattern: weigh sth against sth / weigh up sth
collocations: weigh up the pros and cons

ex.base: Policymakers must weigh the economic benefits against the environmental costs.
ex.past: The committee weighed the evidence before making its final decision.
ex.part: Both sides of the argument must be carefully weighed.

def: To become larger in difference or range

ex.base: The gap between rich and poor widens during economic downturns.
ex.past: The trade deficit widened to eight per cent of GDP.
ex.part: Income inequality has widened in most developed countries.

def: To become or make something worse

ex.base: Air quality worsens in winter when people burn more fuel.
ex.past: Living conditions worsened after the main factory closed.
ex.part: The shortage of teachers has worsened in rural areas.

def: To produce a result, piece of information or amount

ex.base: The new method yields more accurate results than previous approaches.
ex.past: The experiment yielded unexpected results that challenged existing theory.
ex.part: The survey has yielded valuable insights into consumer behaviour.
